lines.text: A thousand islands, a Roman emperor's palace and a merchant republic, then empires, Yugoslavia and a war for freedom. This is the story of Croatia.
Around the year 300, the Roman emperor Diocletian built a vast palace by the sea. Its walls still hold the old town of Split.
The Croats settled here in the six hundreds, and in 925 Tomislav was crowned king. Croatia had begun.
Its medieval kingdom lasted almost two centuries, until in 1102 it joined the crown of Hungary.
By the end of the ten hundreds Zagreb appears in the records, the city that would become Croatia's capital.
On the coast, Dubrovnik grew rich as the Republic of Ragusa, a free merchant state that kept its independence for centuries.
In Split, the poet Marko Marulic wrote in his own tongue and became the father of Croatian literature.
Faust Vrancic, an inventor of the late fifteen hundreds, drew one of the earliest designs for a parachute.
And in the sixteen hundreds, Croatian soldiers wore scarves around their necks. Europe copied them, and the necktie was born.
Ruder Boskovic of Dubrovnik, a scientist of the seventeen hundreds, was a pioneer of the theory of atoms.
Nikola Tesla was born here in 1856. In America he built the alternating-current motors and power systems that light the world.
Josip Broz Tito, born in Croatia, led the partisans in the Second World War and then ruled Yugoslavia until his death.
Franjo Tudjman would become the first president of an independent Croatia.
In the war, from 1941 to 1945, the Nazis set up a puppet state here, one of the darkest chapters in Croatia's history.
In 1949 the Plitvice Lakes became a national park, sixteen lakes joined by waterfalls in the forest.
Inside Yugoslavia, the Croatian Spring of 1971 called for reform and more freedom, until it was put down.
Goran Ivanisevic would later win Wimbledon in 2001, as a wild card no one expected.
And Luka Modric, a boy of the war years, would become a great midfielder and win the Ballon d'Or in 2018.
In 1991 Croatia declared independence, and war followed. It lasted four years.
The Yugoslav army shelled Dubrovnik, striking the old town that had stood for centuries.
In August 1995 Operation Storm retook the Krajina. The war ended, and some two hundred thousand Serbs fled.
In 2013 Croatia became the twenty-eighth member of the European Union.
Five years later, the small nation reached the World Cup final in Moscow, losing to France but winning the hearts of many.
And on New Year's Day 2023, Croatia took up the euro and opened its borders in the Schengen area.
From Diocletian's walls to the heart of Europe, Croatia's story goes on.
